# Common Irregular Present Tense — The Verbs You Can't Avoid

## Overview
These are the most frequently used irregular verbs in Spanish. They break the regular conjugation patterns from A-01, but they appear in nearly every conversation. Rather than memorizing rules, the learner must internalize these forms through sheer repetition and usage. Grouped by irregularity type, these verbs unlock the ability to talk about wanting, being able to, going, knowing, having, making, and saying — the core actions of daily life.

## When to Teach
- Phase: A
- Prerequisites: A-01-present-regular
- L1 interference to preempt: none specific (irregularity is universal across languages)

## The Pattern

### Group 1: Stem-Changing e→ie

The **e** in the stem changes to **ie** in all forms EXCEPT nosotros and vosotros (the "boot" pattern — the changed forms form a boot shape in the conjugation table).

#### querer (to want / to love)

| Person | Pronoun | Conjugation |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| 1st singular | yo | qu**ie**ro |
| 2nd singular | tú | qu**ie**res |
| 3rd singular | él / ella / usted | qu**ie**re |
| 1st plural | nosotros/as | qu**e**remos |
| 2nd plural | vosotros/as | qu**e**réis |
| 3rd plural | ellos / ellas / ustedes | qu**ie**ren |

#### tener (to have) — also yo-irregular

| Person | Pronoun | Conjugation |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| 1st singular | yo | t**eng**o |
| 2nd singular | tú | t**ie**nes |
| 3rd singular | él / ella / usted | t**ie**ne |
| 1st plural | nosotros/as | t**e**nemos |
| 2nd plural | vosotros/as | t**e**néis |
| 3rd plural | ellos / ellas / ustedes | t**ie**nen |

> **Note:** Tener is doubly irregular — stem-changing (e→ie) AND yo-irregular (tengo). The yo form must be memorized separately.

### Group 2: Stem-Changing o→ue

The **o** in the stem changes to **ue** in all forms except nosotros and vosotros (same boot pattern).

#### poder (to be able to / can)

| Person | Pronoun | Conjugation |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| 1st singular | yo | p**ue**do |
| 2nd singular | tú | p**ue**des |
| 3rd singular | él / ella / usted | p**ue**de |
| 1st plural | nosotros/as | p**o**demos |
| 2nd plural | vosotros/as | p**o**déis |
| 3rd plural | ellos / ellas / ustedes | p**ue**den |

### Group 3: Yo-Irregular (First Person Only)

These verbs have an irregular **yo** form but conjugate normally in all other persons.

| Verb | Meaning | Yo form | Other forms regular? |
|------|---------|---------|---------------------|
| **hacer** | to do / to make | **hago** | sí: haces, hace, hacemos, hacéis, hacen |
| **saber** | to know (facts) | **sé** | sí: sabes, sabe, sabemos, sabéis, saben |
| **conocer** | to know (people/places) | **conozco** | sí: conoces, conoce, conocemos, conocéis, conocen |
| **salir** | to leave / go out | **salgo** | sí: sales, sale, salimos, salís, salen |
| **poner** | to put / to place | **pongo** | sí: pones, pone, ponemos, ponéis, ponen |

> **Key pattern:** Many yo-irregular verbs add a **-g-** in the first person: hago, salgo, pongo, tengo. Recognizing this pattern reduces the memorization load.

### Group 4: Fully Irregular

These verbs have unpredictable forms that must be memorized.

#### ir (to go)

| Person | Pronoun | Conjugation |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| 1st singular | yo | **voy** |
| 2nd singular | tú | **vas** |
| 3rd singular | él / ella / usted | **va** |
| 1st plural | nosotros/as | **vamos** |
| 2nd plural | vosotros/as | **vais** |
| 3rd plural | ellos / ellas / ustedes | **van** |

#### decir (to say / to tell) — stem-changing e→i + yo-irregular

| Person | Pronoun | Conjugation |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| 1st singular | yo | **digo** |
| 2nd singular | tú | d**i**ces |
| 3rd singular | él / ella / usted | d**i**ce |
| 1st plural | nosotros/as | d**e**cimos |
| 2nd plural | vosotros/as | d**e**cís |
| 3rd plural | ellos / ellas / ustedes | d**i**cen |

### Group 5: Special — hay

**Hay** means both "there is" and "there are." It is an invariable form of the verb haber — it NEVER changes regardless of whether the following noun is singular or plural.

- **Hay** un problema. (There is a problem.)
- **Hay** muchos problemas. (There are many problems.)
- ¿**Hay** leche? (Is there milk?)
- No **hay** tiempo. (There is no time.)

> **Critical:** Hay is always hay. Never *hayen, *han, or *hayan for "there are."

### Saber vs Conocer — Two Kinds of "To Know"

| Verb | Used for | Example |
|------|----------|---------|
| **saber** | Facts, information, how to do something | **Sé** la respuesta. (I know the answer.) |
| | | **Sé** nadar. (I know how to swim.) |
| **conocer** | People, places, familiarity with things | **Conozco** a María. (I know Maria.) |
| | | **Conozco** bien la ciudad. (I know the city well.) |

> **Rule of thumb:** If you can replace "know" with "am familiar with," use conocer. If you can replace "know" with "have the information" or "know how to," use saber. Note: conocer uses personal **a** before people — "Conozco **a** María."

### Tener Expressions — Where English Uses "To Be"

Spanish uses **tener** (to have) where English uses "to be" for many physical states and sensations:

| Spanish | Literal | English |
|---------|---------|---------|
| tener hambre | to have hunger | to be hungry |
| tener sed | to have thirst | to be thirsty |
| tener sueño | to have sleepiness | to be sleepy |
| tener frío | to have cold | to be cold |
| tener calor | to have heat | to be hot |
| tener razón | to have reason | to be right |
| tener miedo | to have fear | to be afraid |
| tener [número] años | to have [number] years | to be [number] years old |

> **Common L1 trap:** "Soy caliente" does NOT mean "I am hot (temperature)" — it has a sexual connotation. The correct form is "Tengo calor." Similarly, "Tengo 25 años," not *"Soy 25 años."

## Examples in Context

1. **Quiero** aprender español porque **tengo** amigos en México. (I want to learn Spanish because I have friends in Mexico.)
2. ¿**Puedes** ayudarme? No **sé** cómo **hacer** esto. (Can you help me? I don't know how to do this.)
3. **Voy** al mercado porque no **hay** leche en casa. (I'm going to the market because there's no milk at home.)
4. Mi hermana **conoce** a un chef famoso y **dice** que su restaurante **es** increíble. (My sister knows a famous chef and says that his restaurant is incredible.)
5. **Tengo** mucha hambre. ¿**Hay** algo de comer? (I'm very hungry. Is there anything to eat?)
6. **Hacemos** ejercicio por la mañana y **salimos** a caminar por la tarde. (We exercise in the morning and go out for a walk in the afternoon.)
7. ¿**Sabes** dónde **pongo** las llaves? Siempre las pierdo. (Do you know where I put the keys? I always lose them.)
8. **Van** a la playa los fines de semana porque **quieren** descansar. (They go to the beach on weekends because they want to rest.)
9. Mi abuelo **tiene** 80 años y **dice** que **tiene** más energía que yo. (My grandfather is 80 years old and says he has more energy than me.)
10. No **puedo** ir a la fiesta. **Tengo** mucho trabajo y **tengo** sueño. (I can't go to the party. I have a lot of work and I'm sleepy.)

## L1 Interference

Irregular verbs exist in English too (go/went, be/am/is/are), so the concept of irregularity is not new. The main interference is not structural but rather a natural tendency to regularize.

**English habit:** Learners apply the regular conjugation patterns from A-01 to irregular verbs, producing logical but incorrect forms.

**Contrast pairs:**

| Regularized error | Correct form | Why |
|-------------------|--------------|-----|
| *haco | **hago** | yo-irregular: -go ending |
| *sabo | **sé** | Fully irregular yo form |
| *teno | **tengo** | yo-irregular: -go ending |
| *io / *ío | **voy** | Ir is completely irregular |
| *deco | **digo** | yo-irregular + stem change |
| *hayen (for "there are") | **hay** | Hay is invariable — always singular |

**Preemption script:** "You've learned the regular patterns, and your brain will want to apply them to every verb. 'Hacer — yo haco?' Nope. These verbs are irregular precisely because they're used so often — high-frequency words resist regularization in every language. The good news: because you'll use them constantly, they'll become automatic faster than regular verbs."

## Common Errors

1. **Regularizing yo forms:** *"Yo haco" (hago), *"Yo sabo" (sé), *"Yo teno" (tengo). Developmental. The learner is applying A-01 patterns. Correct by drilling the yo forms as a set: hago, sé, conozco, salgo, pongo, tengo, digo.
2. **Pluralizing hay:** *"Hayen tres gatos" or *"Han tres gatos." L1 interference / overgeneralization. In English, "there is" becomes "there are" — learners expect the same change. Drill: "Hay un gato. Hay tres gatos. Hay cien gatos. Always hay."
3. **Saber/conocer confusion:** *"Sé a María" (should be Conozco a María), *"Conozco la respuesta" (should be Sé la respuesta). Developmental. English uses one verb "know" for both. Drill with contrast pairs until the distinction is intuitive.
4. **Tener expressions with ser/estar:** *"Soy hambre" or *"Estoy hambriento" instead of "Tengo hambre." L1 interference. English says "I am hungry" — learner reaches for ser/estar. Teach tener expressions as fixed phrases.
5. **Forgetting stem changes in boot forms:** *"Ella quere" instead of "Ella quiere," *"Él pode" instead of "Él puede." Developmental. The boot pattern (change everywhere except nosotros/vosotros) takes time to internalize.

## Teaching Sequence

### Stage 1: Noticing
Teach in groups, starting with stem-changing verbs (most predictable pattern). Show 6 sentences using querer with different subjects. Ask the learner to find the pattern:

- Yo quiero café.
- Tú quieres agua.
- Ella quiere té.
- Nosotros queremos jugo.
- Ellos quieren leche.

Ask: "Look at the stem — what changes? Where does it NOT change?" Guide toward the boot pattern. Then show poder side by side — "Same pattern, different vowel change."

### Stage 2: Controlled Practice
Conjugation drills by group. Start with stem-changing (querer, poder), then yo-irregular (hacer, saber, conocer, salir, poner), then fully irregular (ir, decir). For each verb, provide the infinitive and a subject — learner supplies the conjugated form. Keep each group to 8-10 items. Then mix: "Translate these sentences using any verb from today."

### Stage 3: Guided Production
Prompt: "What do you want to do this weekend? What can you do? What do you have to do?" This naturally requires querer, poder, tener que, ir, hacer, and saber in context. Provide a verb bank if needed but remove it as the learner gains confidence. Recast regularized forms without interrupting: if the learner says *"haco," respond naturally with "Ah, ¿haces ejercicio? Yo también hago ejercicio los sábados."

### Stage 4: Communicative Practice
Prompt: "Plan a trip together — where do we go, what do we want to see, what can we do there, what do we need to know?" This requires ir (vamos a...), querer (queremos ver...), poder (podemos visitar...), hacer (hacemos una excursión), saber (¿sabes si...?), conocer (¿conoces la ciudad?), tener (tenemos tres días), and hay (hay un museo). Focus is entirely on meaning — planning a real trip — while the irregular verbs arise naturally.

## Dialect Notes
Irregular conjugations are consistent across all major Spanish dialects. As with regular verbs, Latin American Spanish uses **ustedes** instead of **vosotros**, so skip vosotros forms in drills if the learner's target is Latin American. The stem changes and yo-irregular patterns remain identical. Note: in some Latin American dialects, vos replaces tú with its own conjugation (e.g., "vos querés" instead of "tú quieres"), but this is addressed in D-05 (register shifting). See `curriculum/dialect-notes.yaml` for regional details.

## Signs of Acquisition
- **Scaffolded:** Conjugates stem-changing and yo-irregular verbs correctly in drills. Can produce all forms of ir and decir when prompted. Distinguishes saber from conocer when given clear contexts.
- **Unscaffolded:** Uses irregular forms correctly in free conversation without pausing to think. Produces tener expressions (tengo hambre, tengo frío) instead of reaching for ser/estar. Uses hay correctly for both singular and plural existence statements.
- **Integrated:** Combines irregular verbs fluently with other structures — "Quiero ir al mercado porque no hay leche y tengo hambre." No regularization errors. Saber/conocer choice is automatic. Tener expressions feel natural rather than translated.

## Connection Points
These verbs appear in nearly every conversation and serve as building blocks for later concepts. **Ir** enables B-11 (ir + a + infinitive for near future) — "Voy a estudiar." **Tener** expressions are high-frequency survival Spanish that the learner will use from day one. **Hacer** is essential for weather expressions (hace calor, hace frío — taught in vocabulary tier 2), age-related expressions, and duration constructions in Phase B. **Saber/conocer** distinction reinforces the pattern of Spanish having two verbs where English has one (parallels ser/estar from A-02). **Poder** + infinitive and **querer** + infinitive are the learner's first modal constructions — foundational for expressing ability and desire. Common regression trigger: when preterite irregular forms are introduced in B-02, learners may confuse present and past stems (hago vs. hice, tengo vs. tuve). Watch for present tense accuracy during preterite acquisition.
